title: The Energy Tax of Living in a New Place
content:
Laura Serbest writing on Instagram:

Before moving abroad, I was really independent. I loved socialising, visiting new places, trying new things. But over the past few years I’ve become so much more anxious and reserved, and I only just realised why.

When you live somewhere familiar, life is second nature. You know the language, the systems, the culture, and the social expectations. You have routines, support and things are predictable.

But when you live abroad, the energy required to participate in life increases. Socialising, going to appointments, buying a coffee, answering the phone. Everything requires so much more planning, energy and courage.

When you’re already mentally exhausted, you have less energy for the things you want and should do. You avoid situations that feel difficult. You become more reserved, less confident, more isolated and less independent.

I’m writing this at the airport after spending 2.5 months in Tokyo and feeling the above acutely. I’ve never been what you’d call outgoing, but after the initial rush of being here wore off after a few weeks, I definitely noticed myself becoming “more reserved, less confident, more isolated and less independent”. Some days, I barely left my apartment because I couldn’t bear summoning the energy to make a plan, negotiate a new restaurant, or figure out how to get from point A to point B on the train. I sought out places that were easy: online ticketing, digital ordering screens, English menus, chain stores & restaurants.

The confidence piece is probably the hardest for me. I have to work hard in social situations with people I don’t know, and doing that in a language I don’t speak and in a cultural context I don’t fully understand is challenging, especially when I need to do it 10 times a day. I rely on humor in situations like these and, well, I don’t know how to be funny in Japan.1 Confidence tends to be a pervasive trait — a dip in one area of your life causes an overall decline across many areas. And all this is coming after living for the past decade in a place where I never felt like I fit in.

Anyway, it’s been eye-opening, this shift in energy & confidence. I’m onto the next place soon, but this is something I definitely need to keep an eye on.

  1. Tbh, I’m barely funny in English on a good day. But it’s the attempt that counts. ↩
